title: A NEW NAME IN THE LEDGER
subtitle: The Deep South, 1865–1877
introBody: Freedom came with a word, not a deed. You are a freedperson in the Deep South, 1865 — no land, no contract, no protection except what you can build. The Freedmen's Bureau is new and underfunded. Planters still hold the land and write the laws. Every week you choose between survival and dignity, and sometimes you cannot have both.
trailFeedOpener: 1865: The war is over. You are free. You are also penniless, landless, and watched.

events.title: Early Reconstruction — a Freedmen's Bureau agent is registering freedpeople to receive a land plot and enter names on a voter roll. A planter's overseer is watching from the road, taking note of every person who steps forward. Word has already come that a man two counties over was burned out the week after he registered. Your spouse is standing just behind you.
events.text: The agent calls your name. The overseer's eyes are on you. Your spouse's hand finds your arm — not pulling you back, not pushing you forward, just there. You have one breath to decide whether to step forward into the line or turn and walk away.

choices.text: Step forward. Give your name. Let the overseer see your face.
choices.result: This person chose to be counted — to make their existence as a rights-bearing person a matter of record even knowing who was watching. That act of presence is not performed bravery; it is a wager of everything they have on the proposition that erasure is a worse fate than danger.

choices.text: Turn and walk away. Your name stays off the roll. The overseer's eyes move on.
choices.result: This person chose to protect what could be protected — a body, a family, a chance to survive into whatever came next. That withdrawal is not defeat accepted; it is a judgment that keeping people alive is its own form of resistance against a system that would rather they be destroyed.

events.title: Sign Here — Or Else
events.text: The planter's overseer drops a labor contract on the table. Under Mississippi's Black Codes, a freedperson without a signed contract can be arrested for vagrancy and leased out as forced labor. The contract gives you a cabin and a share of the harvest — but you cannot leave without permission.

choices.text: Sign. Keep the family fed and stay out of jail.
choices.result: The ink dries. Your wife exhales. Your neighbor watches from the porch and says nothing — he won't sign, and now he stands alone.

choices.text: Refuse. Walk to the Bureau office and file a complaint.
choices.result: The Bureau agent writes it down. Others see you walk in. Your family goes hungry another week, but word travels that someone pushed back.

choices.text: Negotiate — ask for cash wages, not shares.
choices.result: The overseer scowls but agrees to a small cash supplement. A modest gain — enough to matter, not enough to threaten.

trivia: Mississippi's 1865 Black Codes required freedpeople to carry written labor contracts or face vagrancy arrest.
The vagrancy clause allowed courts to lease arrested freedpeople to planters as forced labor — continuing slavery in everything but name.

events.title: The Schoolroom
events.text: The Freedmen's Bureau has opened a schoolroom in the church. Your youngest child could attend. The planter has let it be known that families who send children to Bureau schools are 'agitators,' and his overseer will remember.

choices.text: Send the children. Education is the whole point of freedom.
choices.result: The children go every morning. The planter's overseer makes note of your name. Your oldest reads back a sentence to you by lamplight, and you have no words for what that costs or what it means.

choices.text: Keep them home. The risk is too real right now.
choices.result: They are safe. The schoolroom fills without them. Your neighbor's daughter learns to read; your child does not — not yet.

choices.text: Send one child, keep one home — split the risk.
choices.result: A compromise that satisfies no one fully. The child who stays asks why. You don't have a clean answer.

trivia: The Freedmen's Bureau established over a thousand schools for formerly enslaved people across the South.
Planters frequently threatened or evicted sharecroppers whose children attended Bureau schools.

events.title: A Torch at the Gate
events.text: A cross is burned at the edge of your property overnight. A note says you have been seen at the Bureau office 'too often.' Your neighbor who registered land last month has already fled north. People on the road are watching to see what you do.

choices.text: Report it to the Bureau agent in the morning — with witnesses.
choices.result: The agent files it. Thaddeus Stevens has been pressing for enforcement legislation in Congress; your report becomes part of the record. Your family sleeps poorly for a month.

choices.text: Say nothing. Pull back from visible activity for a season.
choices.result: The riders do not return. But others who were watching you for courage stop watching — they needed someone to stand, and you stepped back.

choices.text: Mention it quietly to a few trusted neighbors, then wait.
choices.result: Word spreads carefully. No one acts, but no one is surprised either. A thin kind of solidarity — better than silence, less than a stand.

trivia: The Ku Klux Klan was founded in 1865 and used murder, arson, and threats to suppress Black voting and officeholding.
Congress passed the Enforcement Acts in 1870–1871 giving federal courts authority to prosecute Klan violence — largely based on documented complaints from freedpeople and Bureau agents.

events.title: Election Day
events.text: Hiram Revels is running for the U.S. Senate seat in Mississippi — the first Black man ever to do so. The polling place is guarded by federal troops today, but a white man on a horse outside is writing down names. The Fifteenth Amendment says you have this right.

choices.text: Walk in and vote. The Amendment is the law.
choices.result: Your name goes in the ledger. Revels wins his seat. The man on the horse writes yours down too. Your wife grips your hand on the walk home.

choices.text: Stay home. The troops won't be here next election.
choices.result: You are right about the troops. Revels still wins today. But you weren't part of it, and the people who risked their names to stand in that line know it.

choices.text: Go to the polling place, watch the line, and leave before voting.
choices.result: You saw it happen. That is something. It is not the same as doing it.

trivia: The Fifteenth Amendment, ratified in 1870, prohibited denying the vote based on race, color, or previous condition of servitude.
Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first Black U.S. Senator in 1870, filling the seat once held by Jefferson Davis.

events.title: The Redeemers Take the Courthouse
events.text: The Redeemer Democrats have won control of the state legislature. Federal troops are thinning out. The Freedmen's Bureau office in town is closing. A planter ally is now the county judge. Everything the last decade built is being dismantled, piece by piece, in plain sight.

choices.text: Organize a petition to Congress through Frederick Douglass's network.
choices.result: Douglass publishes the petition. Congress barely notices. But the document exists — a record that people here named what was being taken from them, and refused to be silent about it.

choices.text: Head north. Get your family out while roads are still open.
choices.result: You go. The people you leave behind watch the wagon roll out. Some will follow. Some cannot. You keep your family whole. You leave the community thinner.

choices.text: Keep your head down and wait to see what happens.
choices.result: What happens is what always happens when no one pushes back. The losses come faster than you expected, and waiting turned out to mean accepting.

trivia: Redeemer Democrats used fraud, intimidation, and violence to retake Southern state governments throughout the 1870s.
The Freedmen's Bureau was effectively shut down by 1872 after Congress repeatedly refused to fund it adequately.

events.title: The Last Federal Troops Leave
events.text: It is 1877. The Compromise has been reached in Washington — the presidency goes to Hayes, and in exchange the last federal troops withdraw from the South. There is no more Bureau. There is no more federal enforcement. Whatever you have built, you built it. Whatever you protected, you protected it yourself. You are not done choosing.

choices.text: Stay. Dig in. What was built here must not be abandoned.
choices.result: The troops leave. You remain. Your family is frightened. Your neighbors see you still standing. Someone has to be the reason others stay. You decide that is you. It will cost something you cannot yet measure.

choices.text: Leave for good. You have kept your family alive — that is enough.
choices.result: You go. Your family is intact. The community you leave behind is diminished by exactly one family that mattered. History will not record which way you turned on this road. You will remember.

choices.text: Wait and see how bad it gets before deciding.
choices.result: The answer comes quickly. 'Wait and see' in 1877 meant watching the doors close one by one and calling the paralysis a plan.

trivia: The Compromise of 1877 ended Reconstruction by withdrawing the last federal troops from the South in exchange for Republican Rutherford Hayes winning the disputed 1876 presidential election.
After federal withdrawal, Southern states systematically dismantled Black political gains through poll taxes, literacy tests, and terror — ushering in the era of Jim Crow.

events.title: A Klan night-riding season begins. Riders are targeting freedpeople who registered land or voted. Your neighbor, who did register, has fled. People are looking to you.

text.default: Your name is on the roll. Everyone knows it — the riders know it, your children know it, the families now sheltering in your dooryard know it. There is nowhere to step back to. The choice made at the Bureau office means you are already the thing they are coming for, and the people around you are gathered to your visible fire whether you invited them or not. Whatever you do next, you do it from that exposed ground.

variants.text: Your name is on the roll. Everyone knows it — the riders know it, your children know it, the families now sheltering in your dooryard know it. There is nowhere to step back to. The choice made at the Bureau office means you are already the thing they are coming for, and the people around you are gathered to your visible fire whether you invited them or not. Whatever you do next, you do it from that exposed ground.

Your name is not on any roll. The riders pass your door. Your children are asleep inside. And your neighbor's empty house is visible from your window — the cost of the choice you did not make, worn by someone else. People are looking to you because you are still here, still standing, still intact, which is its own kind of statement in a season that is emptying the county of everyone who stood in the open. What you do next, you do from that surviving ground.

choices.text: Go on.

sages.name: Oliver Otis Howard
sages.title: Commissioner, Freedmen's Bureau
sages.bio: General Oliver Otis Howard commanded the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands from 1865 to 1872. A devout Christian and Union war hero, he genuinely believed in the Bureau's mission but repeatedly ran into presidential opposition, underfunding, and the limits of federal will.
sages.greeting: The Bureau agent in the next county says a man named Howard is coming through personally. He arrives on horseback, dusty, with a missing right arm from the war. He shakes your hand with his left.
sages.advice: "We have courts, agents, and some authority — for now. Use it. File every complaint, document every violation. The paper record is the only thing that survives when the politics shift."

question.question: What was the primary purpose of the Freedmen's Bureau?
choices: To redistribute all plantation land equally to formerly enslaved people
To help freedpeople negotiate labor contracts, access courts, and establish schools
To register freedpeople as citizens and issue them federal identity papers
To recruit Black soldiers into the permanent U.S. Army
question.explanation: The Freedmen's Bureau mediated labor disputes, set up schools, and gave freedpeople limited access to federal courts. It did not redistribute land — the famous 'forty acres' plan was blocked by President Johnson. Its authority depended entirely on federal funding and political will, both of which steadily eroded.
question.teksRef: TEKS 8.9 — Reconstruction: federal protection of freedpeople and the role of the Freedmen's Bureau

portraitAttribution.artist: Mathew Brady (1823?–1896) or Levin C. Handy (1855?–1932)

sages.name: Hiram Revels
sages.title: AME Minister & U.S. Senator, Mississippi
sages.bio: Hiram Revels was an AME minister born free in North Carolina who became the first Black U.S. Senator in 1870, filling the Mississippi seat formerly held by Jefferson Davis. He advocated for freedpeople's rights and the integration of Washington D.C. schools before his term ended in 1871.
sages.greeting: You see him at the church after the Sunday service — a measured man in a good coat, shaking hands carefully. He asks your name and actually listens for the answer.
sages.advice: "The vote is a lever. It only moves things if you use it, and they know that — which is exactly why they want to take it from you. Use it while the law protects it."

question.question: Which constitutional amendment gave Black men the right to vote?
choices: The Thirteenth Amendment
The Fourteenth Amendment
The Fifteenth Amendment
The First Amendment
question.explanation: The Fifteenth Amendment, ratified in 1870, prohibited denying the vote based on race, color, or previous condition of servitude. The Thirteenth abolished slavery; the Fourteenth granted citizenship and equal protection. Together these three Reconstruction Amendments reshaped the Constitution — until Southern states found extralegal ways to circumvent them.
question.teksRef: TEKS 8.9 — Reconstruction Amendments and Black political participation

sages.name: Frederick Douglass
sages.title: Abolitionist, Journalist & Public Advocate
sages.bio: Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in 1838 and became the foremost Black public intellectual of the 19th century. During Reconstruction he pressed relentlessly for full citizenship, voting rights, and land access — and watched with mounting anger as federal resolve collapsed in the 1870s.
sages.greeting: His speech is already finished when you find a seat near the back. Afterward he moves through the crowd, and for a moment you are face to face with someone who has been naming this thing your whole life.
sages.advice: "The problem is not that America does not know what justice looks like. The problem is that it has chosen, repeatedly and deliberately, to look away. Do not let it forget what it chose."

question.question: What ended Reconstruction and withdrew the last federal protections from freedpeople in the South?
choices: The Supreme Court struck down the Thirteenth Amendment
The Compromise of 1877 traded federal troop withdrawal for a Republican presidential victory
President Grant ordered the army home after the Klan was fully defeated
Congress passed a law abolishing the Freedmen's Bureau and ending martial law
question.explanation: The disputed 1876 presidential election ended in the Compromise of 1877: Rutherford Hayes received the presidency, and in exchange the last federal troops were withdrawn from the South. Without enforcement, Redeemer governments dismantled Black political gains rapidly, launching the Jim Crow era that would last nearly a century.
question.teksRef: TEKS 8.9 — Collapse of Reconstruction and the Compromise of 1877

route.title: The Deep South, 1865–1877
route.description: Twelve years of Reconstruction — hope, resistance, and retreat.

eventTrivia.question: What did Mississippi's Black Codes require freedpeople to carry at all times?
choices: A signed labor contract
A federal passport
A Bureau identification card
eventTrivia.fact: Mississippi's 1865 Black Codes required freedpeople to have signed annual labor contracts. Without one, they could be arrested for vagrancy and leased back to planters as forced labor.

eventTrivia.question: Which federal agency set up schools and labor courts for freedpeople after the Civil War?
choices: The Department of the Interior
The Freedmen's Bureau
The Union Army Signal Corps
eventTrivia.fact: The Freedmen's Bureau, established in 1865, negotiated labor contracts, set up courts, and founded over a thousand schools for formerly enslaved people across the South.

eventTrivia.question: What did the Thirteenth Amendment do?
choices: Granted Black men the right to vote
Abolished slavery throughout the United States
Guaranteed equal protection under the law
eventTrivia.fact: The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified in December 1865, abolished slavery and involuntary servitude in the United States except as punishment for a crime.

eventTrivia.question: Which amendment granted citizenship and equal protection to all people born in the United States?
choices: The Thirteenth Amendment
The Fifteenth Amendment
The Fourteenth Amendment
eventTrivia.fact: The Fourteenth Amendment, ratified in 1868, granted citizenship to all persons born or naturalized in the U.S. and guaranteed equal protection of the laws — a direct response to Black Codes that denied freedpeople basic rights.

eventTrivia.question: What was the Ku Klux Klan's primary goal during Reconstruction?
choices: To restore the Confederacy's military forces
To suppress Black voting, officeholding, and education through terror
To negotiate labor rates for white sharecroppers
eventTrivia.fact: The KKK used murder, arson, and beatings to drive Black voters and officeholders from public life, targeting anyone associated with the Republican Party, the Bureau, or freedpeople's schools.

eventTrivia.question: What were the Enforcement Acts of 1870–1871 designed to do?
choices: Fund the Freedmen's Bureau for another decade
Give federal courts power to prosecute Klan violence against Black citizens
Redistribute abandoned plantation land to freedpeople
eventTrivia.fact: The Enforcement Acts gave federal courts jurisdiction over civil rights violations and Klan terrorism, allowing the Grant administration to prosecute hundreds of Klan members — a rare instance of federal action that briefly slowed the violence.

eventTrivia.question: Hiram Revels of Mississippi became notable during Reconstruction because he was the first Black man to do what?
choices: Serve as a U.S. Senator
Command a Union Army regiment
Head the Freedmen's Bureau
eventTrivia.fact: Hiram Revels was elected to the U.S. Senate in 1870, filling the Mississippi seat once held by Confederate president Jefferson Davis — a deeply symbolic inversion of the postwar order.

eventTrivia.question: What did the Compromise of 1877 trade in exchange for a Republican presidential victory?
choices: New railroad land grants in the South
Withdrawal of the last federal troops from Southern states
Federal funding to rebuild Southern courthouses
eventTrivia.fact: The Compromise of 1877 resolved the disputed 1876 election by giving Rutherford Hayes the presidency; in exchange, federal troops were withdrawn from the South, ending Reconstruction and leaving freedpeople without federal protection.

eventTrivia.question: What was 'sharecropping' and why did it trap freedpeople economically?
choices: A system where freedpeople owned land but shared profits with the government
A labor system where workers farmed a planter's land and owed most of the crop as rent, keeping them perpetually indebted
A federal program that divided plantations into equal plots for freedpeople
eventTrivia.fact: Under sharecropping, freedpeople farmed plots on a planter's land and paid a large share of their harvest as rent, often buying supplies on credit from the planter's store. Debt compounded each year, making it nearly impossible to save, buy land, or leave.

eventTrivia.question: Who was Benjamin G. Humphreys, and what was his role in limiting Black freedom?
choices: A Union general who enforced the Reconstruction Amendments in Mississippi
The governor of Mississippi who engineered the 1865 Black Codes to re-impose unfree labor on freedpeople
A Freedmen's Bureau commissioner who oversaw land redistribution
eventTrivia.fact: Benjamin Humphreys, Mississippi's first postwar governor, pushed through the 1865 Black Codes — laws requiring labor contracts, restricting movement, and criminalizing vagrancy — to restore planter control over Black labor without formally reinstating slavery.

eventTrivia.question: Why did Thaddeus Stevens and Radical Republicans want a more thorough Reconstruction than President Johnson?
choices: They wanted to punish the South with permanent military occupation
They believed lasting freedom required land redistribution and federal enforcement of civil rights
They wanted to annex Southern states as federal territories permanently
eventTrivia.fact: Stevens argued that without land and legal equality, emancipation was hollow. He pushed for the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments and the Reconstruction Acts over Johnson's vetoes, believing political and economic power for freedpeople was the only guarantee of genuine freedom.

eventTrivia.question: What did 'Redeemer' Democrats mean when they said they were 'redeeming' Southern states?
choices: Restoring white Democratic political control by overturning Reconstruction governments
Repaying war debts to Northern banks on behalf of freedpeople
Reforming corrupt Republican state governments through honest elections
eventTrivia.fact: Redeemer Democrats used the word to frame their campaign as rescuing the South from 'Black Republican' rule. In practice, it meant systematic fraud, intimidation, and violence to dismantle Black political participation and return planters to power.

eventTrivia.question: Which three amendments ratified during Reconstruction are sometimes called the 'Reconstruction Amendments'?
choices: The First, Second, and Third Amendments
The Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments
The Tenth, Eleventh, and Twelfth Amendments
eventTrivia.fact: The Thirteenth (1865), Fourteenth (1868), and Fifteenth (1870) Amendments abolished slavery, guaranteed citizenship and equal protection, and protected Black male voting rights respectively — reshaping the Constitution before Southern states found extralegal ways to circumvent all three.

eventTrivia.question: What methods did Southern states use AFTER Reconstruction to prevent Black citizens from voting?
choices: They passed new constitutional amendments reversing the Fifteenth Amendment
They used poll taxes, literacy tests, and racial terror to disenfranchise Black voters
They petitioned the Supreme Court to void the Reconstruction Amendments
eventTrivia.fact: Poll taxes required payment to vote; literacy tests were administered selectively to disqualify Black applicants; and continued violence from groups like the Klan made voting physically dangerous. Together these tools produced the Jim Crow era that lasted until the Voting Rights Act of 1965.

eventTrivia.question: What was the 'forty acres and a mule' promise, and what happened to it?
choices: A successful federal land program that gave freedpeople homesteads in the Midwest
A plan to distribute confiscated Confederate land to freedpeople, blocked by President Johnson who restored the land to planters
A promise made by Confederate officers to Black soldiers who switched sides
eventTrivia.fact: General Sherman's Special Field Order No. 15 set aside coastal land for freedpeople in 40-acre plots. President Johnson reversed the order in 1865, restoring confiscated land to pardoned Confederate planters. Freedpeople who had already begun farming the plots were evicted.

eventTrivia.question: Why was Frederick Douglass an important voice during Reconstruction?
choices: He commanded federal troops enforcing the Reconstruction Acts in Mississippi
As a formerly enslaved man and leading Black journalist, he publicly demanded full citizenship and land rights for freedpeople
He negotiated the Compromise of 1877 on behalf of Black communities
eventTrivia.fact: Douglass used his newspapers, speeches, and political connections to hold Reconstruction to its promise. He criticized both Southern resistance and Northern retreat, arguing that without enforceable rights and economic power, emancipation would be replaced by a new form of servitude.

historicalContext: Reconstruction lasted from 1865 to 1877. During its height, freedpeople voted, held office, built schools, and negotiated labor contracts with federal backing. The Freedmen's Bureau aided millions. Hiram Revels and other Black politicians served in Congress. But President Johnson's vetoes, chronic Bureau underfunding, Klan terror, and the Compromise of 1877 — which withdrew the last federal troops from the South — ended the experiment. By 1877, Redeemer Democrats had retaken every Southern statehouse. Poll taxes, literacy tests, and racial violence produced Jim Crow, which would not be dismantled for nearly another century.

verdict.good: You stood in that line, filed those complaints, sent your children to school, and put your name on the petition when it would have been easier — and safer — not to. None of it was safe. The troops still left in 1877. The Redeemers took the courthouse. The rights you exercised on paper were stripped in practice before the ink was dry. Reconstruction failed — not because people like you didn't fight for it, but because the country decided not to back them up. You were on the right side of a fight that was lost anyway. That matters. History remembers the Reconstruction era's freedpeople as the ones who built schools, cast votes, and ran for office under conditions that were meant to make all of it impossible. You were one of them.
verdict.bad: Every time the choice came, you chose the path that kept you safer and left others more exposed. Not cruelly — carefully. You signed the contract that let your neighbor stand alone. You stayed home on election day. You pulled back when the riders burned the cross. You were not wrong to be afraid; the fear was real and the danger was real. But fear was the reason given, and the choice was still made. The rights that Reconstruction briefly secured — the schools, the votes, the courts — required people to hold the line under exactly the pressure you faced. They needed you. You were there. You were just looking out for your own, and in the end, that meant looking away from everyone else's.
verdict.indifferent: You moved through twelve years of Reconstruction without ever quite committing to any of it. Not to the people who needed someone to stand, not to the family that needed someone to stay. You took the wait-and-see when the choice was hard, the split-the-risk when the moment asked for more. The Compromise of 1877 came anyway. The troops left. The courthouse changed hands. All the things that were built and all the things that were lost happened around you, and you were present for all of it without being part of any of it. History did not record where you stood in this moment. You were there, and you coasted through it. That is its own kind of answer.

reviewSummary:
Reconstruction ran from 1865 to 1877, and for freedpeople in the Deep South it was twelve years of building something real on ground that kept shifting beneath them. Freedom came with the Thirteenth Amendment in December 1865, but it arrived without land. President Johnson reversed General Sherman's plan to distribute confiscated Confederate land in 40-acre plots, restoring the property to pardoned planters and leaving freedpeople landless. Mississippi and other Southern states responded immediately with the Black Codes — laws requiring freedpeople to carry signed annual labor contracts, criminalizing vagrancy, and allowing courts to lease arrested freedpeople back to planters as forced labor. Governor Benjamin Humphreys of Mississippi was the architect of these codes, which restored planter control over Black labor in everything but name.

The Freedmen's Bureau, headed by Commissioner Oliver Otis Howard, gave freedpeople limited but real tools: labor courts to contest unfair contracts, agents to file complaints against planters, and over a thousand schools where children and adults learned to read. Planters consistently threatened families who used Bureau schools or courts, and Congress chronically underfunded the agency. The Fourteenth Amendment in 1868 guaranteed citizenship and equal protection; the Fifteenth Amendment in 1870 prohibited denying the vote on account of race. Hiram Revels of Mississippi became the first Black U.S. Senator that year, filling the seat once held by Jefferson Davis.

The Ku Klux Klan used murder, arson, and beatings to suppress Black voting and officeholding. The Enforcement Acts of 1870–1871 gave federal courts power to prosecute Klan violence, and the Grant administration briefly used them. But Republican resolve was fading. Redeemer Democrats — who framed their campaign as rescuing the South from Republican rule — retook state governments through fraud and terror throughout the 1870s. The Freedmen's Bureau effectively closed by 1872. The end came with the Compromise of 1877: Rutherford Hayes received the disputed presidency, and in exchange the last federal troops withdrew from the South. Without enforcement, poll taxes, literacy tests, and continued racial violence produced the Jim Crow era, dismantling the Reconstruction Amendments in practice for nearly another century.
